utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I make sure first that I am being heard by everyone, the appellant included, in his own language? Thank you. Will the Registrar call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT 94-1-A, the Prosecutor versus Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May the Chamber have the appearances?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Good afternoon, your Honours. For the Prosecution I am Michael Keegan, I am assisted this afternoon by my colleagues Miss Ann Sutherland and Mr Payam Akhavan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And for the appellant?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours. I am Milan Vujin and with me today is Mr John Livingston on behalf of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The court is sitting today pursuant to an order which the Chamber made on 24th November 1997 by which it appointed today as a day on which we would hear the appellant's motion of 6th October for leave to produce additional evidence. I would skip much of the procedural history of the matter, this being well known to the parties. I would merely say that it appears to us there are three appeals, two concerning the conviction of the appellant and one concerning the sentence passed on him. The appeal briefs in all three matters have been filed on 12th of this month, subject to a question which the Prosecution may wish urgently to consider, as to whether their brief includes the list of authorities visualised by the Rules. Today's proceedings do not concern the appeal relating to sentence. They concern only the outstanding motion relating to the admission of additional evidence. A motion for extension of time to file the appeal briefs may, I think, be considered as spent. The Tribunal then has before it the appellant's motion on 6th October 1997, the Prosecution's response of 20th October, and we have also seen the Prosecution's memorandum on law dated 21st of this month. We appreciate how disorienting it can be to a member of the bar to come to the bar table with a structured presentation in his mind and then to discover that the court would wish him to proceed along some other lines, so that is not our disposition this afternoon. You will be free to present your cases as you see fit, but it may be helpful to you in helping the bench if you would bear in mind some of the issues thrown up by what I may call, roughly, the pleadings; that is to say the appellant's motion and the Prosecution's response, coupled with the proceedings of the Status Conference which was held on 19th September. We think that it would help us if the parties would address some of those issues, and they are as follows in my mind: the question of the meaning of the words "not available" in Rule 115(A), and in particular where the material is not available, where it was in fact available but due diligence may not have been exercised. Again, is material not available where the failure to present it to the lower court was due to a mistake on the part of counsel. Again, does the Rule visualise that the bench should have before it full copies of the proposed additional evidence so as to be able to assess it and to determine whether it meets the criteria which the bench may extrapolate from the law with your assistance. Is it credible, does it touch any of the issues raised in the court below? Does it establish the innocence of the appellant, or does it go towards showing that there is substantial doubt on the findings of the lower court? Those are by no means exhaustively stated items. My colleagues will be throwing in their bit as we go along, they will be asking questions quite freely, and we would therefore welcome your assistance in the resolution of these and other problems. Now a housekeeping matter concerns the availability of time. We have read the documentation which you have so thoughtfully laid before us. We suppose, of course, that each side would wish to add or to explain something in the material which it has laid over with the court, and we are in your hands, except that I would propose this for your consideration. Would it be all right, do you think, if we allocated one hour to each side to make its presentation, and then there could be a second round with ten minutes or fifteen minutes on each side; allowing, of course, for interchanges between bench and bar in the usual way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That is acceptable to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That is acceptable to the Prosecution; and the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: It is acceptable for the Defence too, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We hope to terminate, if I may put this to you as an outside mark, by 6.00 pm, when some of the members of the bench have another official occasion to attend within the precincts of the Tribunal. So now, may I invite the appellant or his counsel to elaborate and to address the court as he sees fit?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. We are, of course, quite prepared to discuss all these points that you as the President of the Trial Chamber have indicated, but we have to say that we have requested with our motion, dated 22nd November, leave for additional time to collect evidence. You have said that we would skip this, so I will not dwell on it too much, but I need to say that this motion of ours referred precisely to the submission of reasons why we need the time we have requested. We do not consider this motion to be our definitive request for the presentation of additional evidence pursuant to Rule 115 of the Rules of Procedure, because reading those Rules and the time limit envisaged in that provision, we feel that we still have the right to amend that request with additional evidence that we managed, in the later time period which was given to us as an extension, that we were able to collect in that period. Therefore, this time allotted to us up to the moment when we had to submit our motion we spent in the field seeking additional evidence which would verify and confirm the defence of the accused, Dusko Tadic. All right, in our first motion for the extension of the time limit for the submission of the appeal, we indicated that we have found traces of additional evidence which call in question the conclusions of the first level Trial Chamber regarding the establishment of facts relating to the activities of the accused, his presence at various events and his participations in the acts for which the judgement has found him guilty. I must point out at the outset that with respect to the words and meaning of the words "unavailable" that you are very well aware that during the beginning and the duration of the trial of the accused, Dusko Tadic, the region in which a part of the events that were discussed in this Trial Chamber took place was still in an extraordinary situation in view of the conflict among the ethnic groups in that area, that afterwards there were political disagreements in that same region, and all this contributed to the inability of the Defence to gain possession of certain documents or of information regarding certain witnesses who could appear before this court. Therefore this word "unavailable" is quite certainly adequate in relation to all the evidence that we have mentioned in our motion for the extension of the time limit, and for all the evidence that we are ready to offer this Trial Chamber today, and if agreement is reached, and I think that there is no doubt that the Rules are not sufficiently precise as to the final limit, time limit for the submission of further additional evidence, in the sense of what your Honour mentioned today, that you need to have full information that we are calling. The question of the validity of those statements will have to be discussed, and we are ready to present them to you even today, because those statements were taken by Defence counsel or their associates. Those statements may be lacking because they were not made under oath as envisaged under the Rules of Procedure. In the oral argument before the President of the then Trial Chamber, Judge Cassese, we had offered already then, together with a representative of the Tribunal and the Prosecution, that we go together to collect testimony from a certain number of witnesses. We stand by that proposal today, pursuant to the provisions of Rule 71. However, as Rule 71 provides that this be done in written form, we have agreed or rather reached agreement with Judge Cassese, he being the presiding judge, that in order to gain time, the Defence should present what it has already at this stage, and that is what we have done in our motion. We are prepared to present today a list of witnesses, which is again not final, bearing in mind the promise made by Mrs Plavsic, the President of Republika Serbska, that she will continue to co-operate with us and help us find additional information and believing that we have a time limit of 15 days prior to the hearing in the Appellate Chamber, we are continuing our work in the field and we continue to keep touch with possible witnesses who were earlier unaccessible and whom we would like to bring to the Tribunal or to take a statement from them in lines with the Rules of Procedure. We hope that the latest political developments will contribute to this end positively. I must also say that this word "unavailable" should also be interpreted bearing in mind that the former police forces in the municipality of Prijedor were those that prohibited contact with certain witnesses whose names we managed to obtain during our investigations in the field. That is one other additional reason why we believe that all evidence was not presented to the Trial Chamber that would be relevant for passing a fair judgement; therefore all the evidence was not presented that would guarantee a fair trial for the accused Dusko Tadic. The Defence in its appeal has also drawn attention to not a mistake of the previous Defence counsel, because we wish to avoid passing any judgement on the work of our colleagues, but at the request of our client, it seems to us that in a part of the proceedings, the accused did not have adequate legal protection, because of the position of the Defence that no Defence should be made for what was related to count 1 of the indictment, that is the act of persecution, because the principle that one witness is not a witness was applied, and that he could therefore not be found guilty of those charges. Having seen a film that was shown on Dutch television on the work of the previous Defence team, and having learnt of certain names that were mentioned as potential witnesses, and which were not available at the time because of the prohibition on the part of Mr Sima Drljaca, chief of police, and partly also because other witnesses were not available because their residence was unknown, we immediately started our investigations and we used to a very extensive extent the data that we were able to collect from the proceedings in the military Tribunal in Banja Luka against the accused Dusko Tadic for the criminal offence of desertion. We were present as Defence counsel at those hearings to the testimony of a number of witnesses and we learnt that a large number of those witnesses in the investigative procedure before the military court have direct knowledge, either as direct participants in the events or as persons who eyewitnessed certain events, about what was happening in Kosarac, Omarska, Keratem, Trnopolje, as to whether the accused was there at all or not, what his views are regarding nationality problems and so on. All these problems were reviewed in the military court and a large number of witnesses were heard and we used a part of those statements, we have collected them, and we are ready to present them to the Chamber in the form in which we receive them, as well as a part of the statements that we received talking to witnesses, and we have those statements in writing, signed by them. Therefore, we managed to discover certain names of witnesses only by attending the proceedings in the military court in Banja Luka. That is also an explanation why we were unable to get the names of those witnesses before because those proceedings were not underway as they are now. As regards the question of the credibility of that evidence, the Defence, together with its appeal, and in addition to indicating the names of witnesses -- for some we used a pseudonym because we feel they need to be given protection -- we have also submitted a large number of written documents that we managed to obtain after hearing these proceedings in the military court, and those documents that have been attached and provided are photocopies of original documents which are at the disposal of this Chamber when they are reviewed and therefore the Defence counsel has nothing against an order by the Chamber for the credibility of these documents to be verified, for these documents to be authenticated. A large number of those documents have to do with medical reports regarding the accused, as well as some witnesses. These are original medical documents of which we have provided the photocopies, and on the basis of which it is possible to link certain allegations of witnesses who are familiar with the facts. Therefore, the position of the Defence is that all the documents submitted are fully credible and authentic and that any rejection of that written evidence would put us in a position not to be able to establish the truth, because a part of them corroborate the alibi used by him in his defence, whereas some of the documents also negate some other facts established by the Trial Chamber. For this reason, the Defence is requesting from the Appeals Chamber leave to give instructions so that a representative of the Tribunal and a representative of the Prosecution and the Defence should jointly interview some witnesses, a list of whom we have today and are ready to provide it to your Honours; however, a part of those statements are in the form I have already described, they are either records taken from the military court in Banja Luka, or a record that we kept, minutes that we kept as Defence counsel, and we are ready to offer them to you now so that these witnesses should be interviewed. We feel that in so doing we would be saving time and resources, because in that case these witnesses would not have to be brought before the Appeals Chamber, since the procedure in the Appeals Chamber applies mutatis mutandis, the same procedure applies as in the Trial Chamber. Mr Livingston -- we will speak in greater detail about this, but we would like to request the assistance of the court should our attempt, our proposal for us to interview these witnesses that we have mentioned jointly, and should that fail, that an order be given to Republika Serbska or some other state, Yugoslavia if any of those witnesses are there, that they have to appear before this Appeals Chamber. What we have offered as additional evidence are statements by witnesses for several of the main events for which the accused has been sentenced by the Trial Chamber. Those are events that took place in Kosarac for which we are offering a series of witnesses who claim opposite to what was alleged by some witnesses during the hearings; that is that Dusko Tadic was present. They are denying that, and we feel that as a Chamber, somehow not hearing the witnesses who have allegations opposite to those made early on, it will not be possible for you to establish whether the Trial Chamber established the truth or not. Let me just give you a small example. The statement of a witness who testified before the Trial Chamber regarding the presence of the accused in Kosarac during the events of 24th to 27th May and she claimed that she had seen the accused Dusko Tadic in a certain situation and from a certain position. That witness also appeared as a witness before a military Tribunal in Lausanne, France, where the accused was Goran Grabez and where that witness claimed that she had seen Goran Grabez in the same period, in Kosarac, whereas the military court in Lausanne established that at that time Grabez was in Austria and Germany, so he could not be there; he had an absolute alibi and Grabez was released. We have offered a photocopy of that judgement of the court in Lausanne and the record, the transcript from the main hearing of that witness, and she claimed there that she saw someone and it was established that she did not, and in this case too, she claims that she saw the accused, then one must call in question her testimony here, the more so as we have offered the names of witnesses who claim that Dusko Tadic at that time was elsewhere and this is corroborated with certain documents and there is no secret in it, we can mention it, that we also have medical documents for his mother, whom he took for check-ups in that period, so these documents corroborate this. I am mentioning this only to illustrate the importance of these elements. If we want the fair trial and if we want to establish the truth, then we need to hear the witnesses that we have now found and any other witnesses that we may discover, taking into account the time that we still have at our disposal prior to the hearing. Those would be our introductory arguments and pleadings why we believe it is absolutely essential that, pursuant to the provisions of Rule 115, you accept our motion, because we consider that this additional evidence is of such probative value that it is absolutely essential that it be admitted. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ascertain from the bench whether we have any questions which we may wish to put to you at this time, or whether we would hold our questions until we shall have heard Mr Livingston. Mr Livingston.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: May it please your Honours. I would like to try and get to the core of the situation which we are in today, and, putting it shortly, although I say this with some regret, I am not sure that your Honours are in a position to deal with the motion to admit the additional evidence today. I say that for this reason: there was I believe a hearing at which I was not present on 19th September, I think before his Honour Judge Cassese alone, where he was faced with an application which was essentially to extend time for filing the appellant's brief. His Honour, and I say quite rightly, pointed out that a good reason had to be provided for granting that extension. There were in fact numerous reasons which could have been given for asking for that extension, a number of which I set out myself in a letter to his Honour Judge Cassese of 7th November, but the particular one that Mr Vujin latched on to on 19th September related to the calling of new or additional evidence in this case. As a result, his Honour Judge Cassese, as I understand it, and I am open to be corrected, because I think Mr Keegan was there that day as well, I am open to be corrected if I am wrong, ordered that some idea be given by the Defence of what that additional evidence was so that some evaluation could be given as to whether it was worthwhile giving an extension of time. Had I been there on 19th September, I would have straight away pointed out that the Defence were not in a position at that time, nor within the time limit allowed for filing of the motion, we were not ready and would not be ready to put in the new evidence in the appropriate form. However, the order having been made, I particularly did my best to comply with it, and hence you have before you what is labelled "motion for the extension of the time limit", and what in essence it does is to try and summarise in as much detail, and I say this because I was primarily responsible for drafting it, as much detail as possible, the essence of the evidence which we anticipated that we would be asking the Trial Chamber to allow the witnesses to give. I should point out immediately that a number of those witnesses had not been properly seen, they had not been properly interviewed at the time, and I would resist any attempt to hold Mr Tadic or his Defence team to any particular statement in that motion. It was stated to be provisional because it could not have been in its final form, and unfortunately, that is the only -- it has been termed hereafter unfortunately as the Rule 115 motion to admit new evidence, but that is the only motion of that sort which you have, and it is specifically stated to be provisional. When Mr Keegan and his colleagues came to reply to that motion, it was not a great surprise to see that he was asking for the evidence to be put in a rather different form. That is something which Mr Vujin and I have been attending to and we now do have -- although these documents, as I understand it, have not yet been submitted to the Prosecution or to the Tribunal -- we now do have proper detailed statements from most of the witnesses who are referred to in that motion of 6th October, and I think I am right in saying, I am sure Mr Vujin will correct me if I am wrong, that we are in a position today to file those statements. I remember, it is not very long ago, so my memory does not have to be that good, but Judge Shahabuddeen did say in opening the proceedings this afternoon that the Tribunal would want to see exactly what the new evidence was going to be. I do not think you can do that, with respect, simply by looking at our motion of 6th October. You would need to be able to look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just a moment. I do not have the perfect power of recall, but I doubt if I ruled on the point. I threw it out as an item for consideration, on which counsel for both sides might wish to address the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: I am grateful for that and I am sorry if I misrepresented your Honour's position, but I think the reality is, any court, any responsible court which is faced with an application to admit new or additional evidence must have that new evidence before it in a proper accurate form, in as detailed a form as the party applying to call it would wish it to be in. Otherwise, I do not think it is possible -- in my submission it is not possible to judge whether it is admissible within the Rules or not. This is why I come back to the point that I opened with, that at the moment, the Tribunal, the Appeals Chamber, does not have that evidence in that form before you. Can I also say this? Although I have indicated that we would be in a position, should the Appeals Chamber, should your Honours order it this afternoon, although we would be in a position to file numerous of those statements, a great many of them are actually still in the Serbo-Croat language, and do need to be translated. It was necessary for the statements to be made in Serbo-Croat I think for the obvious reason that it was important that the witnesses should be able to read them themselves and feel confident about signing them at the end, but many of them have not been translated and they plainly would need to be translated. My submission is that until those statements have been filed, until Mr Keegan and his team have had a chance to look at them, after, of course, they have been translated, we cannot actually take this question of the motion to admit the new evidence any further at the moment. Can I also say this? This question of the new or additional evidence is related to certain other matters which are before the Appeals Chamber. Notably, it is related very much to the request for binding orders which your Honours will be aware were filed back in November, because one of the reasons why we have not filed what I would call a proper motion to admit new evidence or additional evidence is because that might have been rather subsumed by what happened to our request for binding orders, because if those are acceded to, there could well be quite a bit of extra additional evidence that we would be applying to put in, and in my submission, it did not make a lot of sense to finalise our position until we knew where the land lay in relation to our request for binding orders. I hope that this Appeals Chamber will deal with that request relating to the binding orders this afternoon, because if they are to be granted, then more work is required and we would like to be able to get on with it, of course, as soon as is possible, but that is clearly a matter which is heavily related to the application for new evidence. Your Honour, what I would ask is that the Appeals Chamber give us some guidance this afternoon, because this is, of course, the first appeal against conviction to come to this Tribunal, as to the future progress of this motion; in other words, setting dates for filing any new statements that the Defence propose to rely on, including translation, for consideration of them by the Prosecution; also to deal with the binding order request, to deal with the matter about which Mr Vujin mentioned, about the Prosecution and the Defence jointly going to Republika Serbska to interview some of the witnesses who are mentioned on the second of the binding order requests. Your Honour, can I say this? I do not particularly want in open session to mention the names, but an indication has certainly been passed to me by all sections of those who are in power in Republika Serbska, and I use that because it may be thought that there are different political factions there, and at times it may be said that it is not clear precisely who is in control of what, but the information has been passed to me from all sides that the granting particularly of the second binding order request which relates to Republika Serbska would be welcomed, and it certainly, as I think I have indicated before in the documentation, there has been a complete absence of voluntary assistance whatsoever, but it is thought that if the court were to make appropriate orders that that co-operation might well be forthcoming. I think I should stress that so that the limitations which the Defence now and even more I think at trial, the limitations which they had to work under I think could now be alleviated if the requests were granted, particularly the second one, accordingly. I do not want to do the binding order matters in open session, I think for reasons which your Honours will be aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: It is ex parte at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Yes. I just thought it was only right to mention it, because it does relate to this whole motion concerning new evidence and what the appropriate time would be to consider it. Can I also say this, that the Prosecution have recently filed a motion which I only saw yesterday relating to the large number of exhibits which are annexed to the appellant's brief. They are, of course, new or additional evidence in the very limited sense that none of them were before the Trial Chamber. I do not think anybody would disagree with that, but I think the Prosecution cannot have it every way here, because initially their complaint was that the Defence had not put in full enough details of the additional evidence that they wanted, that was the response to 6th October motion. Now that we have put in much fuller information, including the annexes to the appellant's brief, it is really a matter now, whatever the procedural situation, it is really a matter now of evaluating that information to see whether it complies with the requirements of Rule 115 or not. I hope that the Appeals Chamber will cut through the technical arguments, whether the Defence may technically be in breach of orders concerning the filing of appellant's briefs; what matters is, what is the evidence that the Defence asks to call and does it comply with Rule 115? The sooner that evidence is before the Appeals Chamber, the better. In my submission, the Defence should not be castigated for lodging that with the appellant's brief. At least it is now with the Prosecution, they are now in a position to look at it and assess it and, of course, it does very much form part of the Rule 115 application, and if the Prosecution and anybody else has not looked at the annexes and considered them, then I do not think again we are in a position to deal with the matter today. There is one final point I would like to make. Served on me this morning, of course, is the memorandum produced by the Prosecution, the legal memorandum about the meaning of Rule 115. I have read it, but I have to say that I have not really had an opportunity to consider it in any great detail, and frankly, I would be rather loath to embark on an argument relating to a very important motion on such very short notice. So your Honours, what I would invite you to do is to give directions today as to the future conduct of a motion to call additional evidence, and that would include, if you see fit, the filing of a proper motion relating to the calling of that new evidence, which in my submission has not actually been done, although various parties seem to be under the impression that it has been. Your Honour, unless there are any other matters which you wish to ask me about at this stage, those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr Livingston. Let me enquire from colleagues whether they would wish to put any questions now or after the Prosecution has replied. Thank you, Mr Livingston. May I invite the Prosecution to address the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Good afternoon. May it please the court. To address just a couple of the housekeeping matters, to inform you, your Honour, the book of authorities was filed at 2.00 this afternoon, so as we were coming into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr Keegan, since it has been filed this afternoon, and since the interval between the filing of the appeal briefs and the filing of the list of authorities is relatively modest, may I, however, enquire from the Defence whether they have a position on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: No, the Defence has had no time to take a position on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Very good. The court will determine its position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Moving on now, your Honour, to the issues of the day, noting your opening remarks, we believe that our memorandum of law which was served on the lead Defence counsel yesterday afternoon addresses the particular questions, our interpretation of international standards on the particular questions you asked. I would simply indicate that the international standards are clear. The two basic requirements for the introduction of new evidence would indicate that first there is in fact a due diligence standard incorporated in the international standards, and the standards incorporated by the majority of states; and that is set out, forth in the international documents by indicating that the unavailability of the evidence at trial cannot be attributed in whole or part to the accused and the defendants, and that the question of the evidence itself, before it could be admitted, it must be of such a nature that it would conclusively show that there has been a miscarriage of justice. I think that those two standards generally address the particular issues that you raised, the four questions about the evidence itself and the question of whether a due diligence standard exists. Further, we would submit that the jurisprudence of this Chamber itself has indicated that that international standard has been in fact adopted already by this Tribunal, in particular obviously in the Erdemovic case as we cited in our brief. The unanimous holding of the Appeals Chamber in that decision clearly indicates that the due diligence standard has been adopted and as well the issue of the material nature of the evidence, put in terms of relevance in that particular judgement, and also, as reflected in the statements, the comments of Judge Cassese to the parties in this particular case during that Status Conference which has been referred to. Moving on now in fact to the Defence's request in this particular case, I note on the one hand that the general content of the Defence's submission here today is that they have been unable to comply with the order of the Appeals Chamber to submit its brief on this question because of an inability to collect the evidence which they would then want to submit with that brief. On the other hand, in the final submissions of Mr Livingston, he indicates that in fact much of that evidence has been included in the appeals brief. We might say that in fact in reading the appeals brief you find that it is in fact the motion for the consideration of new evidence itself as opposed to a brief that addresses the particular issues on appeal that were raised by the Defence in their Notice of Appeal. That is what prompted our motion for a clarification. So the Prosecution is now prepared today to deal with the state of the Defence's request for new evidence as it stands now, and that includes an incorporation to a degree of the material submitted with the appeals brief. If we use the submission in October, filed in accordance with the instructions of Judge Cassese as the framework, we are prepared to address each of the sections and compare them against the standards which would be required for a consideration of that material as appropriate to be submitted as new evidence. If we start then with paragraph A of the Defence brief, where they contend that there is an issue of mistaken identity, of confusion with respect to the appellant for the crimes for which he was convicted. The Defence contends that there is a confusion by the witnesses in the identity and state that one Miso Danicic in fact made a voluntary confession to a -- this Miso Danicic made a voluntary confession to a Serbian journalist in August 1995 that he in fact had committed the crimes and that the Defence were unaware of this until Lubimir Tadic was approached by the journalist, allegedly in March 1995. In fact, we submit this evidence was well known to the Defence at the trial, and I would briefly cite to the following extracts of evidence which are part of the appellate record. 19th June 1996, Mr Wladimiroff cross-examines a witness, asking him: "Do you know Mr Danicic, or a person called Mr Danicic?" On 17th July, another witness again asked whether he knows Miso Danicic. On 18th July in cross-examination, Mr Kay, in questioning a witness, indicates to the witness, makes the suggestion that she in fact was mistaken when she says she identified Dusko Tadic in Omarska and then Mr Kay then puts to her: "What I would like to put to you is this, do you know a man called Miso Danicic?" Again on 19th July, a witness is asked the same question, 24th July --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise for the interruption, but if I may make an objection? Mr Keegan has entered into a deliberation of evidence which may be presented. I thought that we had agreed that in our statements, we present our general positions regarding Rule 115. We have stated loud and clear that we do not still consider having made a motion for the presentation of new evidence, bearing in mind the time limit for that, according to Rule 115. It is not correct to say that Judge Cassese had given us an order to submit a brief with additional evidence. We were given instructions to submit a motion for the extension of the time limit and to illustrate in it what we had done and what we intend to do. So our objection would be that we do not dwell on individual aspects of that motion, but only when we hear when you will consider the date for our submission of the request for additional evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I need to intervene here, for purposes of clarification. I do have to confess to you that my own understanding of the status of our proceedings today, and I believe I reflect the views of colleagues, was that we were going to listen to a motion for leave to admit additional evidence under Rule 115. Now, if there is no such motion before the Appeals Chamber today, then what is the nature of the motion that we are debating? Does it come under any Rule which makes the hearing a cognisable hearing, a competent hearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Perhaps I can answer that. Your Honour. The position I think is this, and I accept it is perhaps a confusing one, but the motion that was filed on 6th October is quite clearly headed, and I was not responsible for heading it, Mr Vujin did that and Mr Vujin was here in September before his Honour Judge Cassese, but it is clearly headed, "Notice for extension of time", words to that effect. There is actually no motion before the court at all headed "motion for the adduction of additional new evidence on appeal". There is no motion which is headed like that whatsoever. What has happened, it seems to me, is that because the reason for extending time to file the appellant's brief that was given in September was the need to obtain and put in proper form new evidence to call on the appeal, and because we were ordered to give an indication of what that evidence might be, that what has been interpreted as a Rule 115 motion was incorporated in that motion to extend time. I do not pretend that there is not an attempt there to deal, for example, with the questions of unavailability to a party at trial and whether the calling of evidence is in the interests of justice, but I do stress that that motion was provisional, and there is certainly no motion in a perfected or final form. Indeed, that remains the case even today, but having said that, I think it is abundantly clear, or it must be abundantly clear to anybody who has read the appellant's brief, that it is a central plank of the appellant's position that he does wish to call further evidence, new evidence on appeal which was unavailable at trial and which it is in the interests of justice that this Appeals Chamber should admit. That is a central plank; the problem is that at the moment, although it seems that the Appeals Chamber has regarded it differently, there is actually no final motion before you. You may say to us, "go away and formulate your final motion". I tried to explain earlier that the reason why it has not been put in a final form is because we took the view, rightly or wrongly, that the Appeals Chamber should deal with the binding order requests before a final motion concerning new evidence was filed, because the answer to the binding order motions might well affect the contents of that motion, and the documents which were submitted with it, for example witness statements. It did not seem to us, and if we were wrong then I am sure you will indicate that, but it did not seem to us that it was particularly helpful to submit a motion for new evidence with documentation which might not end up being complete, and then have to ask again after the binding order matter has been dealt with to call further new evidence or make a new application. So that is the reason why there has been no final motion put before you, but I do not want you to be under any misapprehension. There is no other motion before you within the Rules. It will be, and I do not pretend that it is not, a Rule 115 motion, but it is just that it is not in its proper form at the moment, for reasons which I hope I have managed to explain. If I have not, then perhaps you would care to ask me any further matters which I can then clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Please would you help the bench to follow what is being said. I understand you to be saying that there has been an evolution in some of the juridical factors which compose the situation. Originally, so I understand you, the question of your being able to produce additional evidence was intended to be the foundation for your request for extension of time to file your appeals briefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So far as we can see, the appeal briefs have been filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So that rationale has terminated its life.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is there any motion now before the court under Rule 115, or was there ever any motion before the court under Rule 115?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: It appears to me that there is not, but, of course, it is the appellant's position that such a motion should be considered, and indeed we have gone a long way down that track already. I say that simply because the motion which was filed and it was not titled by me, it was titled, "Notice of motion to extend time", and that is plainly not a motion under Rule 115, although the justification given for the application to extend time was that there was a desire to invoke Rule 115, but it does not actually appear to me, although I appreciate it has been assumed by many people that there is a Rule 115 motion in existence at the moment, though as I hope I have made clear there is a wish to make such an application, and it may be that it can all be short circuited, since a number of the matters are raised in the earlier motion of 6th October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Should the bench understand you -- Mr Vujin, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should like to present my understanding of this discussion that we are having today, namely when we discussed the matter with Judge Cassese, we came to the conclusion that there was some imprecision in Rule 115, and that is why some preliminary steps need to be taken, which means if the Defence, pursuant to provision 115(A), is able to submit a motion for the introduction of new evidence, and if such a motion has to be submitted to the court and the other parties 15 days before the hearing in the Appeals Chamber, then we believe that we still have some time available, and it cannot be otherwise, but what we would like is to assist the bench and all of us here in promoting the efficiency of the proceedings by reaching agreement as to the form in which that evidence needs to be presented to this court, so that it might decide whether that evidence can significantly affect the judgement of the Trial Chamber. We believe, because at this stage it is only us that -- only we are familiar with the contents of the witnesses' statements, we believe that those statements absolutely call in question the conclusions reached by the Trial Chamber, so that brings us to the question of whether this Appeals Chamber will accept as relevant evidence what we are offering straight away now, and those are the statements of witnesses, some of which have been translated, others are still in Serbian, and we wish to present them to you and the Prosecution. This is only a part of the witnesses' testimony that we have in our possession, but it is up to you to tell us "we accept that as evidence", that is all. Or we have to find a form together, some way in which that evidence can become relevant, and it can be relevant only if the witness makes that statement under oath. For that, we have two possibilities; either to use the provisions of Article 71 to interview the witness out of court, in the presence of the Prosecution and the Defence, to make that evidence relevant; or it can be by video conferencing or by his actual presence in court, so we have those three possibilities. We have the statements here; if you wish, we wish to give them to you straight away through the Registry, with the help of the usher -- will you please be kind enough, Mr Usher, to accept these exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: My colleague Judge Cassese will pose a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr President. Actually, since my name has been mentioned many times, I would like to clarify what I think to be best of my recollection I stated in the Status Conference, in the closed session. I do not have the transcript of our hearing close at hand, so I am quoting from memory. We can check up afterwards. What I intended to say, and I think I did say on that occasion, was that -- I tried to draw the attention of both parties, in particular the appellant, to the distinction between Rule 115 and 116. At that stage, counsel for the appellant was insisting on an extension of a time limit, and I said, "look, under Rule 116 you have, if you want to get an extension of a time limit, you have to show a good cause", and I said, "in practice, I see from what you are saying that actually your good cause would be the need to produce new evidence", so therefore we move from 116 to 115. In any case, to be on the safe side, we decided, I think the Appeals Chamber decided to grant the extension of time limits. However, I made it very clear that you had to put in a motion under Rule 115 requesting leave to produce additional evidence, so I am afraid you were under a misunderstanding or confusion between these two different Rules which were applicable, but I think I made it very clear and actually, although the motion submitted on 6th October 1997 is titled, "Motion for the extension of the time limit", it is very clear if you read from the first line that this is a motion under Rule 115, so the title is a sort of misnomer. I do not know whether it can be called a misnomer. It is mistitled. The substance of the motion is a motion relating to a request for the production of additional evidence. I think this is important, and I think that since we have to stick to the general principle of international law relating to international proceedings, international trials, whereby no formalism must be banned from international proceedings, I think we should consider, this is my humble view, the Appeals Chamber should consider the substance of this motion filed on 6th October and consider it as a motion under Rule 115, as is clearly stated on page 1 of your motion. The question therefore now arises of whether or not we have to go through this motion, hear both parties and then decide on the substance of the motion and the arguments, oral arguments made by both parties before the bench today, or whether we may decide that we need further documents, for instance the witness statements and so on. But let us -- to my mind, Mr President, I think we should be clear about this particular problem. The motion is before the bench, and is as a motion based, I am sorry to repeat it again, based on Rule 115.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just deal with that? I am quite happy that that, of course, should be the case, and since I drafted most of that particular motion, I am well aware of its contents and I am well aware that it was geared up to dealing with compliance with Rule 115. I think what your Honour has to understand though -- this is why I stressed it was a great pity that I was not here in September, because it was impossible for us to draft at that time a proper Rule 115 notice. I do stress that we did our best in the circumstances to comply with your Honour's order and all you have is a summary of what we anticipated the witnesses would say. Things have moved on since then, and Mr Vujin has handed in a bundle of statements today which are statements by a number of the witnesses who are referred to in what we will now call the Rule 115 motion. Mr Keegan is starting off to try to pick us off point by point according to the motion of 6th October. The fact of the matter is that there are a number of points which are contained in the 6th October motion which we no longer pursue, because the witnesses have actually told us something different from what we expected, and that was the problem, that was always the problem about having to file the motion at what was really too early a stage for us to do it properly, and I am concerned about argument taking place on the basis of statements in the 6th October motion which have now been superseded by what is in the statements which Mr Vujin has handed in a short time ago. It seems to me that if the motion is to be considered properly, it must be done on the basis of the evidence which we actually wish to call, not summaries which are to some extent -- they were the best we could do at the time, but were based on either inadequate interviews or telephone conversations or whatever with witnesses and which were not the subject of full instructions. That is why it was expressly said to be provisional, and that is why, even if one does regard that as a proper Rule 115 motion, one should not simply look at the new evidence in terms of what is set out in each of the paragraphs of the motion, because it is simply not the appellant's position today. Things have moved on, the statements are there and that is what we are actually asking the Appeals Chamber for leave to admit; not the matters which are summarised in that motion of 6th October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr Livingston --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do apologise, but it is very important for us to know what the position of the Chamber is, what is evidence? If these written statements are acceptable as evidence, we can give them today and we can discuss them pursuant to Rule 115. That is what we need to know first. Otherwise we cannot talk about Rule 115 because you do not have the contents of the new evidence, and then how will you be able to assess whether that evidence is relevant in terms of justice. That is the main problem, and it is not true that we agreed to prepare it as a motion under Rule 115, but this was rather an illustration of our request for the extension of the time limit; but if you accept this evidence, then everything is fine and we can continue the discussion. If you say that this is not evidence, that you need to study it, then please let us determine how we should deal with these witnesses, so that their statements and their testimonies should be relevant and only then you can discuss; of course, accompanied with our oral arguments, we would need another public hearing in that case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, Mr Vujin, Judge Cassese confirms the impression which I conveyed to you, that the understanding of members of the Chamber was that we were coming to sit here today on a motion for leave to admit additional evidence. That was indeed our understanding, as Judge Cassese confirms. But we have received a contrary impression from counsel for the appellant, which is to the effect that the present motion is not a Rule 115 motion. My question to you was that if you confirm that, then it would appear to me that since you are master of your own motion, that you yourself consider there is no motion before the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I simply say this? I am quite content to adopt Judge Cassese's reasoning and accept that there is a Rule 115 motion in front of the court. I am quite happy to do that. All I want to make clear is the limits of the motion that was filed. That is my point, that it is a Rule 115 motion wrapped up in a Rule 116 motion, if you want to call it that, and one has to understand the limitations of that. The purpose of the contents were to try and get an extension of time, not as much geared up to a final concluded hearing on a motion to admit new evidence. That is the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right. Well, I will not pretend to be able at this moment to fathom all the niceties concerning the provisional character of the motion. I am content with your acceptance of this motion as a Rule 115 motion and I would at that point therefore turn the matter back to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: But your Honour, before Mr Keegan resumes I do want to point out that although you can treat it as a Rule 115 motion, you should not be holding the Defence to the details of it, which is what, of course, Mr Keegan was starting to go through and that is the problem, because the evidence which we actually rely on is evidence that he has not seen. That is the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. Let us see how far he goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I must confess that the assertions of counsel catch me a bit by surprise. We see that there are perhaps only a couple of ways to proceed today, given their many qualifications on where we are with this proceeding. The first would be, of course, the scheduling order of 24th November is quite clear as to what we were going to do here today, and that was to deal with the motion under Rule 115, so the fact that there was no communication, at least as far as we are aware, that the Defence did not find that that was the status of their motion sort of indicates to us that they believed at least or should have understood that this was a 115 motion that we would consider today. If the Defence is now submitting that the state of the evidence as it existed in their October filing has changed, we could perhaps then consider that the appeals brief is, if you will, a de facto submission on the 115 motion, since it certainly does not address the points of appeal. Rather it seems to be totally consumed with the issue of new evidence; some 600 pages, plus 230 pages of assertions by counsel. The Prosecution would be prepared to proceed with arguments relative to whether or not the Defence has met their burden on this issue by simply asking the Defence to affirm if the categories to which -- or should I say the issues that this evidence is intended to address remain the same as identified in their 6th October motion. If that in fact is the case, mistaken identity and so forth, the Prosecution believes in fact that it does not matter under the standards for admission of new evidence quite frankly what the state of their new evidence is, since they cannot even meet the minimum standards contained within the availability issue, and that is that these matters were fully addressed at trial and therefore additional evidence at this point would not be acceptable in any event. So if that is the case, we are prepared to proceed in that fashion, your Honour. The converse of that, your Honour, I am sorry, is if the Defence are now indicating that they have additional areas, it seems to me that the best the Prosecution can do to assist this Chamber would be to address the areas which they do admit their evidence is relevant to, and then we would somehow need additional time to respond to the other areas they now indicate, so if the Defence could at least indicate if their evidence is addressed on the same areas raised in the 6th October filing, we are prepared to continue with our submissions indicating why that any additional evidence at this point would not satisfy the burden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me understand you, Mr Keegan. You are inviting your colleagues on the other side of the bar to indicate to you whether the additional material they have concerns the particular issues raised in their motion of 6th October?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And if they did that, you would be prepared to receive the additional material, to seek the leave of the court for further time, to respond to that material and then what the court should resume thereafter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, sir, not quite. What I am suggesting is if the issues they prepare to address with respect to the judgement remain exactly the same, it is the Prosecution's submission it does not matter what their new evidence is, it would not satisfy the criteria to be admitted as additional evidence because all of those areas were completely addressed at the trial phase and therefore under international standards additional evidence would not be acceptable at this stage, period. We do not even need to concern ourselves with what their supposed new evidence is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right. Additional evidence would in your view be not legally acceptable at this stage, but the Prosecution offers no objection to the proposed statements being submitted by counsel for the appellant, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In fact we do, your Honour, in this sense. One, we find that these submissions are entirely untimely and there is absolutely no justification for the actions here today in this submission. Second, we would object if they are now attempting to raise additional issues with respect to the judgement which they want to bring forward evidence under 115, again because it is entirely untimely, the Defence being certainly on ample notification that the issue had been joined and that the Appeals Chamber expected to hear argument on this issue, so what I am suggesting is that if the Defence agrees or will substantiate that the sole grounds for the admission of new evidence are the grounds which are listed in 6th October, the Prosecution is prepared to proceed with its argument to assist this court in reaching a determination that this Chamber does not need to see any additional material because the matters are not such for which additional evidence would be acceptable at this stage, because all of the matters raised in their 6th October brief were clearly adjudicated at the trial level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You want your colleagues to respond to you as to whether the additional material about which they have been speaking expands on or is restricted to the points of law which were raised in their original motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, to say I am surprised by the position of the Prosecution, it is to put it mildly. It is unacceptable to such a degree that I think it does not even deserve any comment. We have stated loud and clear in our motion of October 6th that it was a motion for the extension of the time limit for our appeals brief, because we are on the trace of new evidence. At the time, we explained what kind of new evidence and why we needed additional time. That time was granted to us. What does the Prosecutor think? What were we supposed to do in that additional time for collecting new evidence, except to collect such new evidence. Does the Prosecutor think that before such a Tribunal a proceeding which wants to be fair should end with only the evidence presented by the Prosecution, because there are 50 or 100 employees, investigators, with the possibility to travel wherever they wish, whereas the Defence has been working with two attorneys and two investigators who are not even able to gain possession of all the documents in Republika Serbska because of the state of war first and later because of the political situation there. Of course, in our appeals brief we clearly indicated our intention to introduce new evidence, that is our right, we are entitled to that, if the Chamber considers this motion to satisfy the requirements of a motion 115. But we still think that according to the Rule we have time up to 15 days prior to the beginning of the hearing to submit all our evidence. This is a right that no one can deprive us of, because it is prescribed, but we were ready to shorten the time. Our client has been in detention for a long time, and we wish to gather more high quality evidence and we claim that we have found such evidence. If we cannot give you today a part of those statements which we have prepared for you, then you will not have any insight as to what we are talking about. If we need to discuss new additional evidence, and to try and show you that this evidence is relevant for a proper judgement, then we have to start straight away, one by one, and that is why I wanted to give you this evidence and to hear your response, whether you will accept this as evidence, because if you are, then we are ready to submit all the witness statements within the time limit envisaged by Rule 115. If this is not the proper evidence, then may the Trial Chamber instruct us how to present that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do I understand you to be saying, Mr Vujin, that although you now accept the motion as a Rule 115 motion, it was not intended originally to file it as such, and consequently the points at issue stated in the original motion were not necessarily exhaustive of all the points you would now like to lay before the Chamber; consequently you cannot give to the Prosecution the undertaking which the Prosecution is seeking, and at this point I would invite my colleague Judge Cassese, who presided over matters previously, to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr President. First of all, just for the record, let me start with a very minor point. I have now the transcript of the closed session and there I, turning to Mr Vujin, I said: "I would like to call on you to file a motion on the Rule 115 where you show good reasons for the necessity to produce new evidence." So it is very clear. Let us leave aside this point. I think now, to save time, I would like to suggest, Mr President, that we should now, this afternoon, in this hearing, try to address some general legal points which in a way are preliminary to the question of whether or not we should then look into the evidence the Defence counsel would like to produce. As was rightly pointed out by the Prosecutor, Rule 115 lays down two tests. One, the additional evidence was not available to the party at the trial, and two, the Appeal Chamber must regard the production of that evidence to be in the interests of justice. I wonder whether we could, this afternoon, discuss these two tests in a way in general terms, with particular reference, however, with the case at hand. For instance, as for the first test, the evidence was not available to the party at the trial. I wonder whether the parties could address the following points: is it possible to say that evidence can be regarded as unavailable if the appellant was unaware of its existence at the time of trial, or if the appellant's lawyers failed to seek out or obtain that evidence. Three, if the appellant's lawyers failed to call witnesses otherwise than with the agreement of the appellant, and four, if the appellant's lawyers were unable to adduce the evidence because the witnesses refused to testify. So at least we could discuss the general legal categories, as it were, so the way the various technical criteria for applying the first test, to see whether there is agreement between the two parties on these particular criteria. These are general criteria, because then if the -- I humbly submit to Mr President, if then the Appeal Chamber eventually decides to request the party or to allow the party to submit this new evidence, then we will at least have a general legal framework to decide upon that issue. As for the second test, in the interests of justice, one criterion for applying this test has been referred to a few minutes ago I think quite properly by the Prosecutor, when he said, "it is important to see whether or not the appellant is raising issues that were adjudicated by the Trial Chamber", whether these are new issues. This is one of the criteria of applying the test of the interests of justice, so therefore we could probably thrash out these various criteria for the application of Rule 115 and in a way we would comply with the request put at the outset by our presiding judge when he said, "let us this afternoon try to discuss the basic criteria for applying Rule 115", and in the light of the various arguments by the parties, we could probably come to some sort of conclusions, at least this would be particularly useful to the bench for making a future decision on the witness statements you intend to produce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Good. May I suggest that this might be a convenient point to take our usual break. I would suggest 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Can I just ask before the court rises, is it still the court's intention to sit until about 6.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Say that again for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Is it still the Chamber's intention to sit until about 6.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: And not after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: If there is a need, we will have to consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: It is simply a matter of my travel arrangements which the Registry downstairs are waiting to hear about, in terms of train times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We do not propose to go up to 6.00. That is a cut-off point beyond which we will not go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: What I am anxious about is that if the Chamber is going to sit until 7.00, I would like to have that in my mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We do not have it in our power to sit until 7.00. Normally we would. (3.40 pm) (A short break) (4.00 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, the sitting is resumed, and we would invite the Prosecution to proceed with its arguments about the elements of the conceptual framework of the matter, and later on we shall return to the question of the statements. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I would then pick up with the questions posed by Judge Cassese with respect to the standards which are incorporated within Rule 115. I note that the categories raised by Judge Cassese match the standards raised in the Defence brief which the Prosecution objected to in our original submission in October. I would suggest that as indicated in our memorandum of law, and in our original response and as I have already reiterated today, the international standards are fairly clear. The standards raised by the Defence on the other hand find no support in large measure in international law or in the law of states. The question of the first criteria was: is the evidence unavailable if the accused and/or Defence were unaware of that evidence? That is in fact part of the issue or questions raised by the standard of due diligence, and that is exactly what that standard is designed to address; that is a question, of course, of fact for the Chamber to determine in deciding that matter. The same for the second criteria, which was if the Defence failed to obtain the evidence, again the question would be: did they exercise due diligence in their investigations and preparation of the case? That, of course, would be determined by the facts presented by the Defence or the moving party, since the burden rests on that party to indicate why their request is in accord with the necessary standards. The third criteria is in fact rather interesting. I think it presents other issues: that is in fact the criteria of when the Defence counsel fail to call evidence without the consent of the accused. That, of course, presumes that there was some discussion about the evidence and there was disagreement. That criteria would seem to us to raise an issue in addition to this question of whether the evidence was unavailable; it raises the other issue of the competency of the counsel in the effect of representation of the accused. That is a second question which would perhaps have to be joined, and in any event it seems that would require first off the accused to establish there had been some knowledge concerning the evidence, and then a decision absent his or her consent not to call that evidence. That burden would seem to have to be overcome first, or establishment of that fact, and then presumably what consequences flow from that determination, if that determination was made by the Chamber, it may affect things other than this issue of new evidence. But it seems that would have to be overcome first before we even got to the question of whether the evidence would be acceptable in any event, because it may get to the issue which we have addressed already, which is that the matter may have been litigated in any event before the chamber in some other fashion, such that this new evidence would not be relevant. The final criteria was if the evidence is in fact known but the witnesses refuse to co-operate. We believe the citations in our memorandum of law address in fact that issue. Certainly national states seem to be in accord that that would not qualify as a category; nor would it generally qualify, we believe, under international standards, because, of course, nowhere in any situation is it a rule or mandate that justice will be perfect, only that justice will be fair, and there are matters that are beyond the boundaries of any of the parties and sometimes even the chambers or the courts involved, so we believe that that, of course, is again another factual matter and it would be up to the moving party to establish the circumstances of that refusal such that it would satisfy the Chamber that it was beyond the normal course of a witness simply not wanting to co-operate, that there was some other extenuating circumstances which made that evidence now warrant, or worthy of being heard as additional evidence. We believe, then, that in fact, rolling those criteria together, they still in essence fall within what we have stated to be the general standards of international law and in fact the standards that have already been applied by this Tribunal. In relation to this particular case, I return to the main issue that we see in the Defence submission of October which is in virtually every case the issues they are attempting to raise as new evidence were issues which were well within the knowledge of the Defence and in fact in virtually every case were raised in trial and dealt with in trial, and so as I indicated earlier, we do not believe that even -- I should say regardless of the nature of their evidence which they purport to have at this stage, it would not matter because they cannot meet that very basic test that it is a matter that was not litigated at the trial level. So we would like to return to that focus and again determine if that is the Defence submission, in which case we are prepared to address that issue. Again, I have tried not to refer directly to the appeals brief, because we, of course, have submitted this other motion to the Chamber with respect to the nature of the appeals brief as it currently stands, but it does bear, I think, comment that there is a substantial amount of new evidence submitted with that appeals brief, and it begs the question of why we are talking about even further additional evidence today; why was it not submitted with the appeals brief; why was that not in fact submitted in total as a submission under 115, which it is in fact at some time by the Defence; why are we now addressing these issues, and we would submit that it now falls on to Defence to indicate why the information in the appeals brief, if it is considered a de facto request to consider new evidence, and this material that they have today, how it meets the standard for admission of new evidence, irregardless of the actual nature of the evidence. Why would it fall within the acceptable standards as they are? Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me see if my colleagues would wish your assistance on any particular points. Judge Mumba will ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr President. In addition to the points that you have made, I would also like to know whether the fact that witnesses who were known by the appellant and who were available, had refused to co-operate or to come forward and give evidence, will be important in a situation where the Defence counsel did not bring that fact to the attention of the Trial Chamber, because we are aware under the Rules that we can have video conferencing, we can have a deposition and things like that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Yes, we believe that that would be one of the main criteria or facts that would have to be established if the Defence was now attempting to put forward evidence on the basis that it was unavailable based on witness non-co-operation. Certainly one of the initial responses of the Prosecution, and we would assume questions from the Chamber would be, what attempts were made to compel the testimony of that witness, or bring the testimony forward in some other form, whether it be by admissions entered into between the parties, for example, or depositions, or any other method to bring forward that evidence. That would be certainly the test or the standard applied to such a request by the Defence. We think that it is a matter of fact that would have to be weighed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ask you one little question. I would wish the Defence to understand that when its turn comes, its assistance on these points would be gratefully appreciated, without my having the necessity of repeating them. Under the Statute, Article 25(1)(a) and (b), there are two grounds of appeal; (a) an error on a question of law and (b) an error of fact. Would I be right in saying that a rule-making power cannot be employed so as to modify or expand those two grounds of appeal as set out in the Statute?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I would like your assistance on this question. What is the meaning of an error of fact in relation to the proposed additional evidence? Does an error of fact necessarily imply that the lower court fell into error in its assessment of the facts then before it, or does it mean that objectively an error of fact has occurred viewing the additional material, irrespective of whether or not the trial court itself made that error? I wonder if my contorted question is somehow clear to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, it is clear. I would submit that reading the Article on its face, it would appear to only until the former, and that is in fact a basis of appeal recognised in most states, and that is that it is actually the conclusions of fact that are incorrect and it is based on the trial record, and that it falls actually under (b), where most states would incorporate this issue of new evidence. That, however, is not universal and it is recognised by some states that when there is a fact which unknown at trial which is so meritorious, or as it is put in the international standard, that it is directly or would show conclusively that there had been a miscarriage of justice, that is sometimes incorporated to address this question of an error of fact, but certainly this article on its face, with the lack of prior jurisprudence to interpret it, would seem to indicate it would be indicated to errors based on the trial record, and that is, if you will, the conclusion of fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So your position would be that additional evidence is not cognisable by the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, that is not exactly what I am saying. What I am saying is that it certainly could be a question particularly indicating that there is a question of law invalidating a decision. That is again a legal conclusion, for example, as to the guilt of an accused on a particular issue and a particular crime or matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is any question of law raised by a proposal to provide additional evidence, which I take it is additional evidence of fact, going to the question whether an accused person had an alibi? That is a question of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, but the issue of the alibi results in a legal determination as to responsibility, so I am simply saying if you read it on its face it would seem to indicate that errors of fact are limited to conclusions based on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right. I have no position on that, I just thought I would benefit from your thinking, as I would from the thinking of Defence counsel. Now the second question I have, I am sorry that you have to be disturbed a second time. Mr Vujin has raised a nice question of law, and that is whether under Rule 115 he is entitled to bring a motion for leave to admit additional evidence up to 15 days before the trial. How should I understand your position? Should I understand it to mean this, that according to you, Mr Vujin may indeed wait until 15 days before trial, but that the Rule provides for one and only one exercise of that right, so that if he exercises it now he may not exercise it later; or should I understand it to mean this, he may exercise it now and he may exercise it later, but if he exercises it later, the bench may take account of the fact that he did exercise it on a prior occasion, or maybe you have another interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, I think that covers the possible courses or interpretations which could be given to that provision. We would think as a general rule in procedural matters before a Chamber, once an issue is joined, that ends, if you will, the right of the party to just open-endedly address that issue. There has to be some conclusion. We would read the Rule to indicate, recognising the unique nature of this jurisdiction, that up to and including 15 days before an issue on appeal is set for hearing, a party has the right to bring in or raise a request to bring forth additional evidence which they have become aware of. We would not read that Rule as an open-ended right to continue to investigate a case, because as was made quite clear we believe in Erdemovic and certainly by Judge Cassese in his comments to the parties here, this Rule in no way envisages trial de novo on appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me put this to you.
