Suppose Mr Vujin was in this position: he makes this motion today, seeking leave of the court to admit additional evidence, the nature of which he discloses both to you and to the bench, and then on the 16th day before trial he finds he has additional material which he did not know of before, and he then comes a second time; what will be your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I think at that point, your Honour, that would be when the sub-paragraph (b) would control the issue and that would be a determination by the Chamber that the consideration of the evidence would be required in the interests of justice. We would certainly not indicate that a party should be cut off by any certain date, but it would certainly be a significant factor in determining of whether the interests of justice require consideration of that new evidence or additional evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One last question. Mr Livingston has referred more than once to the question of binding orders being issued by the Appeals Chamber. In your view, is there any provision in the Statute or in the Rules which confers a competence on the Appeals Chamber to issue instruments in the nature of binding orders to assist an appellant in investigating whether he could have evidence which would meet the requirements of Rule 115? Is there any provision which empowers the Appeals Chamber to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. On this particular issue, I believe as raised by the Defence both in the Status Conference and I think they have made mention of it here today, Rule 107, which indicates that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence apply mutatis mutandis to issues on appeal, certainly because in a trial level there would be authority -- actually under a number of Rules, but certainly Rule 54 would authorise the issue of a binding order in certain circumstances to assist the Defence in obtaining evidence. We think that under Rule 107 that would also authorise this Chamber to issue the same type of order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So you would support the Defence on that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That the authority exists. Whether it is justified in this case we would not agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you care to consider a proposition like this: that those wide powers under Rule 54 et cetera which apply mutatis mutandis in relation to the Appeals Chamber only apply insofar as it could be demonstrated that the Appeals Chamber has a particular competence, so the question could be this: has the Appeals Chamber a competence to engage in the investigation of an issue as to whether an appellant could possess himself of evidential material which satisfies the requirements of Article 115? Has the Appeals Chamber that investigative competence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I think that under Articles 25 and 26, and their complementary Rules, 115, and for Article 26, 119 and the following Rules --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You are going very fast for me. 25 and 26, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Both of which give the rights to parties to raise issues on appeal. 115 indicates that the judges of the Tribunal believe that Article 25 incorporates within it the right to bring forward new evidence. If that is the case, then it must be the case that the Appeals Chamber would have the competence to assist the parties in obtaining that evidence when necessary under Rule 107.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Very good. I thank you, Mr Keegan. I would ask the Defence to bear in mind the questions which I have put to the Prosecution and no doubt to take advantage of the support which counsel for the Prosecution has offered to the Defence on the point last discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, bearing in mind what you told the Defence now, in terms of this same question, we have been asked to state our views on it. With regard to this last issue that was put to the Prosecutor and where the Prosecutor supported what the Defence said, we absolutely accept what the presiding judge of the Chamber said and what the Prosecutor said, namely that in terms of 107, you do have the right to give binding orders and you also have the right to see whether it would be in the interests of justice to present certain additional evidence before this Chamber. However, as regards to the answer to the first two questions that you put, your Honour, I think that these are issues to which the Defence sought answers at this point in time, and I think that the Prosecutor is quite wrong in the presentation of his views. First and foremost, the Prosecutor believes that errors of fact can be established only on the basis of what is written down in the transcript of the trial before the Trial Chamber. Such a standpoint is quite unacceptable and it is not applicable in a single system of law. Your Honours, I must say one thing. This is an international court, and we must certainly bear in mind international law, but first and foremost, this is a criminal court, and we have to bear in mind the rules of criminal procedure and criminal law as such, which is not that highly developed in the international sense, but it is certain that the basic postulates are valid, and that is that the right of the defendant to appeal is precisely the right which entitles him to investigate further, after he was pronounced guilty during the trial, and to try to find new evidence which was not available during the first trial. The errors of the Trial Chamber that we pointed out in our appeal, basing our motion on Article 25 of the Statute, that is errors of fact and errors in law, and we are not interested in the application of law in this particular case, but we are interested in errors of fact. I do apologise, I do not want to plead on that and I said we would not, but if the defendant has been pronounced guilty of having slaughtered two policemen, you read that, and the Trial Chamber established that and he was not even charged with that, then that has to be a miscarriage of justice, because he cannot be pronounced guilty of something he was not even charged with in the indictment. However, at this point of law what we are interested in is that a fact was established only on the basis of the statement of one witness that the defendant did that. There is the statement of another witness in the files, who claimed that these people were not killed in the way in which the first witness had said, but that they were killed in a quite different way, by a different person and in a different place. The Defence -- after the proceedings started before the military court in Banja Luka against Dusko Tadic came to new witnesses, three new witnesses corroborate the statement made by the second witness, namely that these policemen were not slaughtered but that these two policemen were killed by firearms. That is the essence of all our proposals in order to introduce new evidence, because all our proposals and new evidence show that there is error of fact, that it was wrongly established, because the court had only one single piece of evidence or only part of the evidence, and now we wish to oppose new evidence to that which is of a far better quality and which entitle you as the Chamber of Appeals, when you are weighing what is the truth, is he himself saying the truth or five other people, that you can then decide whether the Trial Chamber made a mistake or not. Our intention is, in the interests of justice, and that is then in the interests of justice, to present this evidence before you so that you can rule on that. All our proposals for new witnesses that have been just mentioned in our motion are aimed at that, so may I reiterate this? The errors made by the Trial Chamber are based on the wrong validation of facts and based on the evidence that was presented and that is why the Trial Chamber was misled. In the interests of justice, one should hear all the people who were eyewitnesses, who saw for themselves what had happened. All our witnesses are such witnesses, they all say, "we were there and we saw such and such a thing". As regards the second question, relating to what I have been insisting on time and again, and that is that neither you, your Honour, or Judge Cassese as the presiding judge that time, cannot change Rule 115 by your orders. Rule 115 is understood by the Defence in the following way. Until the deadline is reached, we have the right to present motions. As we present one motion, we should not be denied our right to file our motions, and more motions until this 15 day deadline, because that is the rule, and that cannot be changed, even by you, the judges, who had adopted these Rules originally, so we can not change it now. That means that when we filed our motion in October and related this to 115, we only illustrated this with our efforts to show already at that point that we have some new evidence, but it would be absurd to say that at that time we had exhausted our right, even if this is taken as a motion to introduce new evidence, because we get additional time for investigation, for exploration, so how have we thus taken advantage of our full time? We gathered a great deal of evidence which is such that it brings into question the ruling of the Trial Chamber. Therefore, as I said, we are prepared to offer this into evidence but I do not know, and that is why we did not officially file a motion related to Rule 115, because I do not know what your standpoint is, what is evidence in terms of new witnesses? Is what we have in our possession sufficient, or will it be necessary to present this in keeping with the Rules? So that is the basic question, and these are our answers to your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr Vujin. I just wish to reassure you that I did not intend to rule on the question as to whether you would have a second or a third right to bring a motion seeking leave to admit additional evidence. It was a question which I raised to seek the benefit of the advice of Prosecution counsel and of yourself. Now should I understand you this way, that an error of fact in Article 25 of the Statute includes not merely an error of fact committed by the trial court on the material which it then had, but it includes any error of fact which objectively exists, viewing the totality of the evidence including the additional evidence; in other words, does it include a factual inaccuracy, whether or not the trial court was guilty of committing an error?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: I am waiting for the translation. Your Honour, you are quite right and that is exactly my point of view. So it is not only an error of fact that the Trial Chamber should have made when assessing the presented evidence, and also there are such errors in the ruling. There is also a factual existence of errors, of inaccuracies, and that is to say that the Trial Chamber ascertained a fact and that it objectively was not such. In order to establish that, one has to present further evidence. Your Honour, had there been evidence of the event that I spoke of, that this was corroborated by ten or fifteen or three witnesses, perhaps the Defence would not have had a chance to deny this. However, if this is based on the statement by one witness and the Defence has statements by four witnesses who objectively present this fact in a different way, then you cannot check this fact, whether it was objectively ascertained or not, without having heard these four witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I just conclude by asking, if I may, Mr Livingston a question which may be pertinent to the jurisdiction from which he comes. Mr Livingston, my mind is open, quite open, on the question as to whether the Appeals Chamber has a competence to engage in the investigative phase of an exercise leading up to a motion seeking leave to admit additional evidence, quite open. The question I want to ask you, and it is a matter of comparative law, is whether in your jurisdiction the Court of Appeal, criminal division, would engage in the investigative aspect of an exercise, leading up to a motion seeking leave to admit additional evidence, or would it confine itself to looking at the motion itself, if and when it has been presented, and ruling on it. I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: I am not sure I can give you a concluded answer to that question, being fired at me at very short notice like that, but I think the reality is that in the United Kingdom, just as I would imagine in most national jurisdictions, the question of applying for subpoenas or binding orders on appeal does not really ever arise. I have to say that I cannot recall a case where anybody in my country has actually asked the Court of Appeal to issue any kind of subpoena for a witness, so the question of whether they could or not is perhaps a moot point. The issue is here, it may not have escaped the Appeals Chamber that tucked away in the appellant's brief, starting I think at page 102, there is a section on abuse of process, which in my submission raises some extremely important issues for this case and for doubtless many other cases in the future. The point, put very shortly for the moment, because I do not want to argue it now, is that there are quite extraordinary difficulties facing Defence teams trying to accumulate evidence in Republika Serbska. This is something which sometimes I find frustrating, but I have been there for about a week every month since August, and it is incredibly difficult gathering evidence there. If you went there, you would realise it pretty quickly, and you would realise what a frustrating experience it is. Let me say this: the conviction of Dusko Tadic by the Trial Chamber has actually made things even more difficult, because I get faced with a man who could help, who, for example, worked on the water pump system in the Omarska camp, who says, "I did not do anything wrong, but I am afraid, what happens if Mr Niemann and his colleagues issue an indictment against me. I am innocent, but so was Dusko Tadic and look what happened to him". This is the sort of situation which one faces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is all of that relevant to my question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: I think it is, with respect, because if there are problems in getting evidence which the Trial Chamber or indeed the Appeals Chamber, for the reasons Mr Keegan I think has already given you, if the Appeals Chamber can assist, then in the interests of justice it must assist, because in my submission the primary criterion for any court considering the admission of new evidence must be the interests of justice, because no responsible court wants a situation to arise whereby it refuses to allow new evidence and then five years later important new material comes to light which shows that the man is innocent. The real question is, is it in the interests of justice and if the Appeals Chamber can assist in obtaining evidence which may well assist an appellant who is in a very difficult position as regards getting his evidence, if they can assist, and in my submission they should, and the English Court of Appeal is simply not faced with that sort of situation, with the fear, the distrust, the lack of co-operation which sadly exists in Bosnia these days, and it is not just in Republika Serbska it is also, in my own personal experience, it is in the federation territory as well and if anybody questions my view, I hope I have made it clear that I am in a position to call evidence to prove everything that I say. I hope that perhaps does answer your question. As far as I am aware, the English Court of Appeal has not been put in that position, but I can certainly check that, given a little bit more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That is your answer, that to the best of your knowledge, the English Court of Appeal has never had to face this situation. It is a very short answer and I appreciate that indeed. For the rest, I think I should assure you that you are in good ground in appealing to this bench, as a responsible bench which has uppermost in its mind the interests of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: I am glad to hear it. Can I just add one other point? His Honour Judge Cassese raised certain points before the break which plainly relate to the various criteria for the admission of new evidence raised in paragraph 2 of what we are calling the Rule 115 motion. I am not sure that Mr Vujin dealt with those, I do not know whether you would wish him to deal with those points or not, or whether he would wish me to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I may explain, in my mind and the minds of my colleagues, you are now in the first part of the second round, you can speak now and then your colleagues can reply to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Yes. Would your Honour just give me one moment. Your Honour, it seems there is a consensus I should deal with those points, so if I may. Looking at paragraph 2 of the new evidence motion, setting out what "unavailable" means, can I start by referring you to Mr Keegan's memorandum on the admission of new evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr Livingston, I may say that while, of course, the bench will be grateful to you for your views, you are now replying to the Prosecution, and we will make an effort to keep within the limits of their own presentation, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: I think implicit in Mr Keegan's presentation is his written document which he puts in. I do not think he would wish you to confine yourself to his oral arguments, I think he would wish you to pay attention to what he has put in writing. He does, for example, quote at page 7 one or two cases, for example, S v De Jager, which without reading he quotes as saying that it requires that the Defence demonstrate some reasonably sufficient explanation why the evidence was not led at trial; 2) that there is a prima facie likelihood of the truth of the evidence; and 3), that the evidence is materially relevant to the outcome of the trial. Then McIntee which follows. Appellate courts will always -- I am being told to slow down, I am sorry. Appellate courts will always receive fresh evidence if it can clearly be shown that failure to receive such evidence might have the result that an unjust conviction or unjust sentence is permitted to stand, and then buckle, which follows that, if in a criminal case the new evidence does not exert such a compelling influence but is, however, of sufficient strength that it might reasonably affect the verdict of a jury, then in my opinion the court may admit that evidence and direct a new trial so that such evidence might be added to the scale and weighed by the trial Tribunal in the light of all the facts. What I submit really emerges from those sort of authorities is that one is looking for a reasonably sufficient explanation, and the primacy should be given to the interests of justice. One should not exclude a piece of evidence which might conclusively prove a defendant's innocence simply because it could be said that it might have been obtained at some earlier point. In my submission, that would be to cause a gross situation where a man would stand convicted and it was not able to be put right because of a technicality. What I would submit is that one must interpret this phrase or this word "unavailable" in a fairly unrestricted way, and I add to that that in this particular situation which one is dealing with in Bosnia, where there are such immense difficulties in gathering evidence, one should not adopt the restrictive criteria which are so often adopted in national courts. Your Honours, in particular his Honour Judge Cassese, who was certainly part of the Appeals Chamber in the Blaskic case when the binding orders decision was made, emphasised in a very different context the very great difference between national law and international law before a Tribunal like this, and I would submit that very much the same applies when it comes to interpreting a phrase like "unavailable to a party at trial". Mr Keegan has set out a number of authorities, most of which are American. These are decisions of national courts, where the difficulties, as I have already said, the difficulties about obtaining and gathering new evidence simply do not exist, so the standards of due diligence are very different, and one should not forget that. Going back to paragraph 2 of the motion relating to new evidence, in my submission there cannot be any problem about (b)(i), 2(b)(i). It was not in existence at the time of trial. (ii) the appellant was unaware of his existence. In my submission, there cannot be a problem about that either, because if the appellant was not aware of the existence of a piece of evidence, for example supposing he had an alibi defence, and there was a witness who could testify as to where he was, but for some reason or other he was wholly unaware of that person's presence at the time of his trial, that person's presence and what that person saw subsequently comes to his attention, in my submission a defendant should not be shut out from calling that evidence if it is viewed as being probative and credible simply because he was unaware of its existence prior to his trial and at his trial. So in my submission, there cannot be any inherent objection to an appellant being able to say that evidence of the existence of which he was unaware was unavailable. In my submission, that is quite proper, a quite proper stance for him to take. If he does not know of its existence, certainly in the context of affairs in Bosnia in 1992, it is very unlikely that his lawyers are going to be aware of it or know where to look for it. Your Honours, the most important category I think, frankly, for the purposes of this appeal is likely to be paragraph 2(b)(iii), which is the question of the appellant's lawyers being unable to adduce the evidence because witnesses felt intimidated. This again is a situation which has not come across in national courts. I think it is quite evident from the documentation that you have that the death of Simo Drljaca in Gradina, which is near Prijedor, in the summer this year, had a very major impact on the minds of witnesses relevant to this case. I make no bones about the fact, and there is reference in the documents before the court to the fact that he and others deliberately intimidated witnesses and threatened to kill them if they made any moves to assist the lawyers or give evidence for Mr Tadic in this case. I should point out that Mr Tadic is in an unique position, I do not think there is any other defendant I am aware of who has been indicted who is in this position. Mr Tadic is a deserter, can I make this clear? He is a deserter from the Bosnian Serb Army. For that reason, he attracts a good deal of odium from his own side, and there are many people who I have tried to talk to -- and again I can call evidence if you require about it -- who I have tried to talk to who say, "why should we help a man who is a traitor to our state, who has let down our country? Why should we put our heads above the parapet and assist such a man?". That is again a problem which any lawyer for Mr Tadic is going to face. If his present legal team -- with colossal effort, may I add -- have managed to obtain evidence which his previous lawyers were unable to obtain, then in my submission he should not be shut out from calling it, provided it is credible on its face and likely to be of sufficient probative value. It is the credibility and the probative value of it at the end of the day which in my submission should govern it. If it is, then granted the very difficult circumstances which face lawyers in these cases, one should not interpret the unavailability criterion against an appellant. So in my submission, (iii) is a category where in the specific circumstances of Bosnia, and I am not wishing to make any submissions on any wider situation than that, and in this appellant's particular situation, bearing in mind that he is treated as a deserter, that there are very big difficulties. As far as (iv) is concerned, again in my submission the crucial point is, if new evidence is obtained which is of sufficient probative value that it throws in doubt the validity of the conclusion, one should not shut it out simply because the previous lawyers failed to seek out that evidence. If they failed to seek it out, the reality was that the appellant could not call it at the trial. If they failed to seek it out but again it is evidence which might show that he was innocent, one should not, in my submission, cut him off and say, "you cannot call that off". Your Honour, again let me take the example of the alibi witness. Supposing there was a failure to find that witness. Previous lawyers failed to take full steps to find that witness, so he was unavailable, he did not give evidence. Supposing he then becomes available, he is discovered when new lawyers, new solicitors, new counsel take over? Is one really to say, particularly in this sort of context, that one should not allow such a witness to give evidence? In my submission, it could create a travesty of justice, and result in an innocent man being convicted. That is plainly the view which is very widely held in Bosnia these days. Paragraph (v) is, as Mr Keegan has I think accepted, an interesting proposition; the appellant's lawyers fail to call the evidence otherwise than with the agreement of the appellant. Again, in my submission one then has to look very carefully at the phrasing of Rule 115, "unavailable to the party". That must in my submission refer to the accused or the defendant himself. There is nothing that Mr Tadic or any other defendant can do to get the evidence. He relies on his lawyers, or investigators in the context of this court, to go out and get the evidence for him, to interview the witnesses. If there was a disagreement and his lawyers did not call that evidence, then in my submission again it is going to be a very harsh court which says that that evidence cannot be called on appeal, because an appellant is faced with a very stark choice. Does he sack his lawyers because he has a disagreement with them, or does he continue because there are many good reasons why he ought to? If he decides to continue then he is stuck with the situation which his lawyers have put him in, so again, what one has to do, in my submission, is to say, in principle, where the facts are supported, that proposition too is an acceptable one and can lead to the conclusion that the evidence was unavailable. It depends on a proper examination of all the circumstances relating to the witness in question, and you cannot do that, in my submission, without looking at the evidence, of course, to see whether it is prima facie credible, whether it is of probative value, and seeing what evidence would be available to suggest that the appellant's lawyers failed to call it. All these matters have to be looked at. You cannot make a decision, in my submission, in a vacuum, without looking at the detailed evidence. All I am submitting is that within all those four categories, the evidence is potentially unavailable to an appellant or to a party at a trial. I do not want to repeat it ad nauseam, but if it has the appropriate probative value and it is prima facie credible then in the interests of avoiding miscarriages of justice, there must be an overwhelming case, in my submission, for allowing that evidence to be considered. It may be -- I am not suggesting it is the case with this particular appeal -- it may be, of course, that it results in a decision that a case has to be remitted back for retrial; that, of course, happens in a number of cases. I am not suggesting that should be the case here, but all options are open. The question is, should one shut out the possibility of that evidence being called? In my submission, where any of those five categories apply, one should not shut out the evidence and one should have one's eye very much on what is the evidence going to prove. If it is true, does it in fact show that this appellant, or shed serious doubt on whether the appellant is really guilty or not? As regards the Article 25 point, my submission would be that either proposition is a correct one, that if the Trial Chamber has made an error in its reasoning, for example made two and two make five within the reasoning, then that would be an error on the facts within the judgement itself. Equally, if it has reached a conclusion which in the light of new evidence is shown to be wrong, that again is an error of fact. One should not simply confine errors of fact to internal errors within the judgement, because otherwise that would make a nonsense of the provisions which are in the Statute and the Rules, as in so many national jurisdictions, allowing appellants to call new evidence. If appellants are to be allowed to call new evidence at all, then in my submission one must take account of the new facts, and if those new facts suggest that a wrong conclusion was reached by the Trial Chamber then that conclusion should be altered, and it should be treated as an error which the Appeals Chamber can deal with and reach a different conclusion upon. Your Honour, unless there are any other particular matters that you would wish me to deal with, those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That ends the second round for the Defence. I would put one little question to you. How do you react to a question like this, that in a system in which the appellant has a right to challenge the conviction on the ground that the conviction was not safe, that arrangement is more open to the view that the Appeal Court could take cognisance of an error of fact revealed by the additional evidence, even though there was no error of fact committed by the lower court; in other words, is a formula structured in terms of a right to challenge a conviction on the ground that it is not safe wider than a formula which is crafted in terms of a right of appeal on the specific grounds of error of law and error of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: My submission would be that in practice -- I take your Honour's point, that in theory, since there is different terminology, it may be possible to envisage cases where a verdict would be regarded as unsafe, where there was not any error of fact or law, but in my submission, in reality, and in practice, it is very difficult to see how a verdict could be -- it is very difficult to see how, if there was an error of fact or an error of law, how it could be safe and in a sense vice versa. If it was regarded as being unsafe, in practice there would in my submission always be an error of fact or law which one could find which would make one think that it was unsafe. Perhaps it is a conclusion which the Trial Chamber makes on the evidence which would point to an unsafe conclusion having been drawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: One last question before I turn the matter over to Judge Cassese. He had asked you a question about a mistake being committed by the trial lawyer, who failed erroneously to call evidence of which he was aware. Now I understand your stand to be this, that the determinative criterion is simply whether the additional evidence discloses either that the man is innocent or casts substantial doubt on his conviction; is that your position? If so, are there any limits to that proposition?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: I think there are. What I have in mind is the sort of proposition which I mentioned much earlier in, for example, the McIntee case, appellate courts will always receive fresh evidence if it can clearly be shown that failure to receive such evidence might have the result that an unsafe conviction may be allowed to stand. Sorry, I am being asked to slow down again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Could I ask you whether there is a qualification to that which says something to the effect that the Court of Appeal may interfere if it has a lurking doubt that injustice had been caused by flagrantly incompetent advocacies; is that an admissible test, would you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: I think it is. I would also with respect emphasise again words which I think I did mention earlier in the De Jager defence, about the Defence having to show there is some reasonably sufficient explanation as to why the evidence was not led. That is the phrase that I think one should be concentrating on as well in terms of a qualification, a break on the interests of justice criterion, particularly in the context of a case in Bosnia. I do stress that in my submission it is wholly unlike any case in any national court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We take your point. Would you answer a question from Judge Cassese?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Of course, if I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr President. I will address the issue of witnesses who allegedly have been intimidated. You allege that some witnesses refused to testify because they were intimidated, testify at trial, before the trial court. They were intimidated by or feared a local chief of police, because this man used to interfere with any potential witness. So I have one question which you could probably answer right away, which is: how many witnesses do you intend to call who were so intimidated? These are two questions which you could answer, probably, if you are granted leave by the Appeals Chamber to submit a brief on this matter, on the matter of additional evidence. These two questions would be: what evidence do you adduce that they were intimidated, and in what respect would their testimony serve the interests of justice by casting serious doubts on the findings of the Trial Chamber. Then a final question. I wonder whether you could answer to my mind a very important question asked by Judge Mumba to the Prosecutor some time ago, namely, if I recall correctly what Judge Mumba said: if a witness was being intimidated at the trial stage, should Defence counsel have drawn the attention of the court to this particular circumstance, attention of the Trial Chamber to that particular circumstance? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: There are a lot of questions there. As far as the first question, which was, I think, how many witnesses, I think Mr Vujin may be able to answer that question better than me, because he has a list in front of him and perhaps he can look at that list now. Can I deal with the last question first, which was also one that her Honour Judge Mumba raised. I would accept that in many national courts it could be said that if a witness has been intimidated, it should be raised with the court. Indeed it might be regarded in certain circumstances as a contempt of court not to do that. The problem is here, which lawyers face in a trial like this, is that if you do that, it gets you as lawyers into even deeper water, because if it is known at all that you have been saying that people have been intimidated, then people become even more reluctant to talk to you, and indeed it is not beyond the realms of fancy, and I have been warned personally that my own personal safety would be in danger if certain courses were adopted. I cannot stress too strongly, it may seem -- people may think this is fanciful, but there are a number, I am not saying this should apply to this whole part of Bosnia, but there are a number of very dangerous people there who are ruthless and who wish to protect their own positions for whatever reason, perhaps they fear prosecution, whatever it is. There are a number of very ruthless people there and one has to be very chary about what steps one takes which might actually increase difficulties in the longer run. It may perhaps deal with the question of intimidation in the immediate context, but it may cause difficulties later on, and I do not think it is as easy as saying, "you should have raised it, you failed to do so and therefore because a witness was intimidated that is not a good reason for saying that the evidence was unavailable". There is no question in this case that a number of these witnesses were intimidated. You ask what evidence that we would wish to call. The reality is that if one looks at the statements, the witnesses whose statements have been handed in today explain that they have been the subject of intimidation, and that that is the reason why they were unwilling to assist the Defence at trial; even some who initially did assist. I do not think it would be right for me perhaps in open court at the risk of endangering such a person, but when it has become publicly known that a person has assisted, there is evidence that pressure has been brought to bear on those individuals and those individuals can give evidence about that, and I would like to think that the Appeals Chamber would accept the evidence that those witnesses would give that they have been intimidated, that they were genuinely in fear, and they have to live in many instances in the communities where the people who are putting them under pressure live. For example, in the villages round about where any of the camps are, in this case, there are villages there, there are witnesses who might give evidence; there are also other people who wish to protect themselves living in those very same villages. It is a very, very difficult problem, and it is one where one must be very, very careful about prejudicing a man like Mr Tadic. Your Honour, I think there may have been other points but I did not manage to get them all down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: There were two points which you might address maybe in a legal brief, if you are going to submit a legal brief, namely what evidence do you adduce that they were intimidated -- you say you can produce evidence to the effect that some witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: I hope I had answered that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And also in what respect would their testimony serve the interests of justice?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Mr Vujin makes the comments that he wants to make, I do not think that you can judge that question without seeing what their evidence is. But I can give you one example. There is evidence in this case, given by some witnesses, about being beaten up in a small room at the end of the corridor in what was called the White House. We have evidence which, if it is accepted, would indicate that nobody was beaten up in that particular room. If that evidence, having looked at it in its totality, is found to be credible for the reasons given by the witness, then in my submission it points quite clearly to there being doubt about whether the witnesses who said they were beaten up and others were beaten up in that room is truthful. If that is right, that should result in an end to the convictions on those particular matters. So the evidence must be judged by looking at the statements and evaluating them, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may I should like to answer directly the questions put by Judge Cassese. The list of witnesses that the Defence intends to call or to interview or to give a binding order for them to come to be heard, we have 40 witnesses. Out of that, eight of them in contact with us stated that they were intimidated and that they did not dare speak to the previous Defence counsel. Then there are 24 witnesses whose addresses were not known to the previous Defence counsel, and we found this out when bodies of the military court looked for certain witnesses, and I must tell you that I come from a system where the court summons the witnesses to appear in court, and when they received those summonses, those subpoenas, they were obliged to come and that is how we learnt about what they knew, who they are, where they lived and so on. The previous Defence counsel could not find them, they did not know where they resided. Among others, we have two witnesses of Muslim ethnic origin who are not living in the territory of Republika Serbska and we have only now discovered where they are and where they live so that we now have the evidence which is in the brief and we can also submit it, because Mr Wladimiroff, as Defence counsel of the accused, referred to this intimidation by Drljaca and we have a report by the investigator, Mr Kostic, and Mr Drazic, who drew up a report saying they were prevented from talking to the witnesses by Simo Drljaca and others said they could not speak because they feared Simo Drljaca. Some other witnesses worked for the police, they were police officers and as such obviously could not speak. We have also spoken to and we are still interviewing people in the field, witnesses who held certain positions in Omarska and Keratem and according to the present chief of police, Dusan Jankovic, they are not prepared to testify, they are afraid for their safety, the safety of their families if they appear in the Tribunal, et cetera. But the witnesses we have offered are ready to testify or have already given us written statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I turn the matter over to the Prosecution for the last leg of our procedures, let me turn to my colleagues and see if there are any other questions. Then I invite the Prosecution to make its final reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I would like to respond to the last series of comments. Of course, the interest of all parties concerning at this Tribunal is that justice be done, for all parties who are concerned. That does not, however, give any party to the proceedings the right to cavil early violate rules and standards of a court, and in particular this court. The Defence so far today has very skilfully avoided the essential issue here, which is their burden to establish that this evidence should be considered by this Tribunal. They have talked about the type of evidence and we have had counsel's submission about difficulties. We have yet to have anything that would qualify as evidence that could be used to satisfy a burden. There are numerous points, but if we are going to talk about the record which they have referred to here, let us make it entirely clear. This issue of intimidation of witnesses was raised in the submission of October 6th, where the Defence asserted that there was evidence of a conversation between Simo Drljaca, a Serbian judge and a journalist, and they give the names of those two individuals. There it is alleged that Simo Drljaca indicated that he intended to stop anyone giving evidence, and if necessary by killing them, because he regarded the defendant as a traitor. In point of fact, these individuals who the Defence identifies as a Serbian judge and journalist were the Defence investigators who were there investigating the case. On the record, as a matter of the record in a report dated 6th February 1996, which was submitted to the Trial Chamber by Mr Orie, a member of the Defence team, they indicated that since 1st February, Mr Drljaca had informed the Defence team, 1st February 1996, that he had had a telephone call from Dr Karadzic, Radovan Karadzic, the then President of Republika Serbska, who had given him permission for the Defence discovery activities. Mr Orie discussed this a bit further and then stated on the record that Defence counsel had come to the conclusion that major obstacles to proceed with their discovery activities have been taken away since February 2nd 1996. Then in the course of the case, the Defence did call some 35 witnesses from the territory of Republika Serbska. The Defence utilised measures of witness protection more frequently than the Prosecution did. In calling these witnesses they made great use of videolink testimony from the territory of Republika Serbska and they in fact called policemen as witnesses from Prijedor, and they produced police records from Prijedor given to them by Mr Drljaca, and had in their possession two letters signed by Mr Drljaca indicating his co-operation. It also raises the issue, without wishing to sound cavalier about it, but if Mr Drljaca seems to be the focus of the Defence issue here, with respect to co-operation, he of course was killed in July 1997. We are now in January 1998. It is unclear to the Prosecution why the Defence in those intervening months has not been able to prepare a comprehensive brief indicating exactly what the nature of evidence is and why it would meet the international standard for consideration by this Tribunal. It is far too late in the game to now try and delay the processes of justice further by this continual reference to evidence which is nothing more than cumulative and which is why the Prosecution would wish to address the issue based on the areas of the judgement which this evidence is supposed to relate to, because if they have been litigated fully, the evidence would not be admissible. The use of national law in the brief, of course, was only meant to indicate that it in fact fully supports the international standards set out in the International Covenant and the European Convention on Human Rights. In the case cited most frequently by the Defence, McIntee, they overlook the most obvious point of the case, which is that the evidence will be received: "... if it can clearly be shown that failure to receive such evidence might ..." result in an unjust conviction. It is the burden of the party to make that clear, which they have failed to do, and we are far too late in the game for them to try and claim that there have been procedural difficulties or practical difficulties to obtain evidence. We believe that the type of submissions the Defence are making is in fact not a request under 115, but a request for a trial de novo, which would in fact under the Rules here amount to more of a request for review under 116 -- excuse me, 119, Article 26, than the question of an appeal under Article 25 and Rule 115. Therein lies my interpretation of Article 25 as raised by your Honour, because Article 25 has to be considered in the context of Article 26 and 119. If the Appeal Chamber is going to accept evidence of fact relative to the issue of the findings, the question of whether it is a safe verdict as raised by your Honour, we think that that would require, in essence, the Appeals Chamber to subsume the standards of Rule 119 into 115 and into Article 25, because that is the standard applied in the international law for that kind of broad-based question of the validity of the judgement as opposed to particular issues of appeal on errors of law or errors of fact. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We are moving on to 6.00 and we shall presently relieve Mr Livingston to catch his aircraft. We hope that his schedule will not be unduly disturbed if we announce this time that we will take exactly five minutes by way of a pause and then we shall return.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise, but in view of the fact that we have gone on to the third round, or that is my understanding, could I respond briefly to the Prosecutor's comment and then afterwards we hear your final word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Perhaps we understand it differently. I understood a while ago that you and Mr Livingston were on the second round, and that I stated, admittedly while you were in train, and therefore when the Prosecution spoke a moment ago, they were speaking for the second time in the second round. But if you would like to have another brief word, certainly, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Precisely when you asked the Prosecutor to make its final remarks, I would like to ask leave to make our final remarks, because we consider what they said was quite unacceptable. Our intention is not to manoeuvre, because the Prosecution keeps changing its thesis. I think that it is incorrect on the part of the Prosecutor to say that we are asking for a retrial and this is closer to the provisions of Rule 119 of the Rules, which is quite clear. If new evidence appears which was not known at the time of the trial during the Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber, then that Rule comes into effect. We have not even reached the Appeals Chamber, so 119 is out of the question, because that has to do with retrial and not the appeals trial. The second position is that we are referring to certain procedural difficulties and that Drljaca had informed the previous Defence team about its position. We are not using those difficulties as an excuse, those difficulties exist and we have found evidence which disproves the positions and the judgements of the Trial Chamber. We have just said that a certain number of witnesses were not available to the previous Defence team due to difficulties that are well known to everyone; because there was a war, afterwards the political disputes and the lack of knowledge of the addresses of the witnesses. Therefore, it is the submission of the Defence that the evidence offered which we wish to present to this Chamber calls in doubt the factual conclusions of the Trial Chamber as well as the legal conclusions, and we would like to request that could you, as an Appeals Chamber, tell us whether we will have your permission to submit the written evidence to you and to set a time limit for us to do so, taking into account Rule 115, which says that we have to submit it not later than 15 days prior to the beginning of hearings of the Appeal, and secondly, could the Defence counsel be told that if you will not accept this as evidence, what is it that you would accept as evidence, whether it would be taking depositions with representatives of the Prosecution, through video conferencing or testimony of witnesses here in court, because without your instructions in that direction, we are unable to finalise our brief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I think we may understand the position to be this, that the Defence has made its final statement in response to the final statement of the Prosecution. On that basis, we would pause for exactly five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before you rise, can I just ask one question? Is the Appeals Chamber proposing to deal this afternoon with the binding orders issue or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We shall give you a reply on our return. (5.45 pm) (A short break) (6.00 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The court would thank both sides and we would announce these decisions now. First, the Defence will submit to the Prosecution and to the court through the usual machinery a copy of the additional statements which it has in mind, in English or in French, within two weeks. Second, within the same time the Defence will submit to the Prosecution and to the court a legal explanatory memorandum. Third, the Prosecution will have two weeks thereafter to respond. Fourth, following on the Prosecution's response, the Defence will have two weeks to reply. Fifth, thereafter, there will be no further oral hearing, the court will issue an order setting out its decision on the motion by the Defence for leave to admit additional evidence. Sixth, as to the requests by the Defence for binding orders, this matter will be dealt with by a separate order to be made by the Appeals Chamber shortly. Seventh, the normal appeal sequences are suspended as from now until the making of the order relating to the request by the Defence for leave to admit additional evidence. At the same time, this is the eighth point, at the same time when that order issues on the matter of additional evidence, the Chamber will also issue a scheduling order as to the further steps which need to be taken inclusive of the resumption of the operation of the normal appeal sequences. Ninth, these announcements will form part of the record of the court and will not be the subject of a separate order. Tenth, if I may add this, so far as the delay on the part of the Prosecution to submit its lists of authorities is concerned, as the bench has heard no complaint on this score, that matter is overlooked and indeed there will be time enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I just, without being impertinent, ask one further question? As regards number five, the further oral hearing, do you envisage hearing further argument at such an oral hearing, or is it simply an oral hearing to announce a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I think there was a misunderstanding, for which I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: It was probably my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The bench does not anticipate that there will be a further oral hearing. The bench will issue a written order in a manner to which Mr Vujin is probably accustomed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: It is just what I had in mind, I hear what Mr Vujin says, just what I had in mind was if any argument was required, for example, about issues to which the evidence goes or anything like that before any decision was taken, the court might wish assistance on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Put it this way, nothing that I have said exhausts or denudes the normal competence of the bench to vary these orders as now announced, if and when it sees fit, and to invite further assistance from counsel if that turns out to be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I clear up just one point and that is point seven, that the normal appeals procedure is suspended until we exchange our briefs? Does that mean that the time period we have to respond to the appeals of the Prosecution will not run, which for us is 30 days, nor will theirs run, their time period that they have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Time is suspended, the running of time is suspended. The running of time will only resume when that order is made.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Sorry, if I may beg the Chamber's indulgence, and only because we see it as a directly related issue on new evidence, and that again is the current content of the appellant's brief, in particular the appendices thereto, which amount, in effect, to submissions of new evidence. Could we -- would it be appropriate to consider that material as part of the material we will be addressing during this current time period, to address the question of new evidence in its entirety; in other words, that the Defence should provide a brief just to find a consideration of the evidence submitted with its appellant brief, as well as the material they are submitting today, we would then respond to that total package as a question relating to new evidence, since we see that in fact as what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr Keegan. I see Mr Vujin on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to say that in view of the contents of our appeals brief and what we have annexed to it, I think it is not necessary for us to annex the supplements annexed to that brief on this occasion, when submitting our motion. I am thinking of the written evidence that we have enclosed with our appeals brief, so I think it is not necessary for us to repeat that same evidence. We will just say in this new motion that this evidence be presented as contained in annexes 1 to 35. I think that would be more practical, do you not agree?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: (Pause). As I understand the position, after a little wrestle with myself and a little huddle with my colleague who knows more of this than I do, I would now proceed to announce that we agree with both sides on the positions which they have taken. I understand also, however, that some of the material which you have submitted is not in any of the two court languages; could this deficiency be remedied, do you think? Within what time?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: I would think the two weeks you have allowed is sufficient for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I am sorry if I was not clear. I, of course, intended not that they would resubmit but include the justification for those annexes in this current motion. That, of course, would then leave the remainder of our motion concerning defects in the brief. If those annexes are removed and we have this issue of the suspension of the response, of course, our response, as we indicated in that motion, would obviously change if those defects as we classified them are clarified by the Defence, so if at all possible if we could also roll in this request for the clarification of the appellant's brief to correspond with the six stated bases for appeal in their Notice of Appeal, then once this issue of new evidence is resolved we will be in a position to address the response to a revised brief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Does the Defence agree to that? It seems not unreasonable to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIN
utterances.text: As far as these proposals are concerned, regarding the translations we will submit the translations within the two weeks as we have said, and we will also abide to what we said were our intentions, so all these are just technical matters as far as I understand them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Both parties are content at this stage? Then we would announce the adjournment of the proceedings and you will hear from us in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just again, before we all go, can I ask one further question, relating to number six, the binding orders which I am particularly concerned about. How shortly is "shortly"? I had thought, bearing in mind they are ex parte motions, initially that you might be going to do it this afternoon. Could I ask for a little bit of clarification about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr Livingston, I am sorry to disappoint you. The word "shortly" was used advisably. It was meant to encompass a situation in which the bench at this time does not itself know exactly what time it will need for the purpose, bearing in mind the various other commitments which its members have within this very Tribunal, of which you may be aware. But maybe in two weeks time?

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: What I had in mind was plainly if your decision was in favour of the appellant, then it does affect your general scheduling order, as you laid it out this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. We understand that, and we will make as much haste as is humanly possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: I am grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So the Appeals Chamber stands adjourned at this time. Thank you very much. (6.15 pm)
